readerTitle: Your new website is four weeks late. Now what?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (배관 서비스 업체 웹사이트, 원예용품점 온라인 숍) · 적용 레슨으로 OPS-05-01(범위·시간·비용)과 OPS-05-05(작은 단계 vs 빅뱅)를 사용
insight: 웹사이트 출시는 '다 갖추고 한 번에 여는 일'이 아니라, 날짜와 예산을 고정하고 범위를 줄여 작은 단계로 여는 일이다.
misconception: 웹사이트는 원하는 기능을 모두 갖춘 완성본으로 한 번에 공개해야 한다. 기능을 빼면 실패한 출시다.

sources.text: 프로젝트 관리의 표준 개념 (범위·시간·비용의 상충 관계, 단계적 출시)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례와 수치(6주 일정, 10주차, 상품 2,000개, 베스트셀러 50개)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계나 연구 인용은 없습니다.
도메인과 이메일 이전처럼 한 번에 전환해야 하는 작업이 있다는 설명은 일반적인 웹 운영 상식 수준으로만 적었습니다. 특정 서비스나 업체의 절차는 언급하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your new website is four weeks late. Now what?
body: Dana runs a five-van plumbing business. In January, her web designer promised a new site in six weeks.

It's now week ten. The site isn't live, the spring ads are already paid for, and the to-do list keeps growing. Sound familiar? This lesson puts two ideas from this unit to work on a very ordinary project.

image.label: Plumber looking at a half-built website on a laptop
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작업복 차림의 배관 업체 사장이 밴 옆에서 노트북을 들여다봄. 화면 속 웹사이트는 절반만 완성되어 'Coming soon' 블록과 빈 상자가 보임. 벽 달력에 빨간 동그라미 여러 개. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The list keeps growing.
body: Dana's spring ads start on March 1 and point to the new site. The budget is spent. Her wish list now includes online booking, a reviews page, a blog and live chat.
The designer says all of it means another six weeks. What should Dana do?

options.text: Keep everything and move the launch to mid-April
options.feedback: She gets the full site but pays for ads that send people to the old one. Moving the date is the costliest lever when the date is tied to money already spent.

options.text: Keep March 1 and launch with services, phone number and a quote form. Add the rest later
options.feedback: This is **scope, time and cost** at work: with time and budget fixed, scope is the lever that moves. She loses features for now, not the spring season.

options.text: Keep everything and the date, and pay the designer extra to work weekends
options.feedback: Adding cost can buy some time, but rushed work on four new features invites bugs right as the ads go live.

cards.title: Fix two, and the third has to give.
body: Every project trades off **scope** (what you deliver), time and cost. Dana's date was fixed by the ads. Her budget was fixed by her bank account. So scope had to move.

The trick is deciding what the site must do on day one. For a plumber, that's simple: show what you fix, where you work, and how to reach you. Booking and reviews help, but nobody fails to call a plumber because there's no blog.

image.label: Triangle with scope, time and cost; scope side shrinking
image.brief: 삼각형 인포그래픽. 꼭짓점에 'Time: fixed (March 1)', 'Cost: fixed', 'Scope: flexible'. 범위 쪽 상자에서 'Blog', 'Live chat', 'Reviews', 'Booking' 카드가 'Later' 상자로 옮겨지는 모습.

cards.title: How should the new site go live?
body: The cut-down site is ready. Later, Dana will add online booking and card payments. Her designer suggests three ways to roll it all out.

options.text: Wait until booking and payments are done, then switch everything on one Monday
options.feedback: One big switch feels clean, but if anything breaks, everything breaks at once and you can't tell which part failed.

options.text: Launch the basic site now, test booking with a few regular customers, then add payments
options.feedback: This is **small steps vs big bang**. Each step is small enough to fix fast, and real customers show problems no test plan finds.

options.text: Keep the new site hidden and test it privately until every feature is perfect
options.feedback: Careful, but private testing misses how real customers behave, and the old site keeps losing leads the whole time.

cards.title: The quote form that went to spam.
body: In the first week, Dana noticed something odd: lots of visits, almost no quote requests. The form worked, but its emails landed in a spam folder.
Because the site was small, the fix took an afternoon. Had booking and payments launched the same day, she would have been hunting for one fault among three new systems while customers waited.
Small steps don't prevent mistakes. They make each mistake **small and easy to find**.

cards.title: Small steps and cut scope have costs.
body: Running old and new pieces side by side takes effort. For a while, some customers book online and some by phone, and staff must handle both.
Some changes can't be split. Moving your web address or email usually has to happen in one go, so plan those carefully.
And "later" needs a date. Write the cut features on a list with a rough timeline, or the booking system you promised yourself never arrives.

cards.title: Now it's a garden centre.
body: You run a garden centre with 2,000 products. You want an online shop open before spring, your busiest season, which starts in eight weeks. Photos and descriptions for every product would take about four months.

options.text: Launch with 50 best-sellers and in-store pickup only. Add delivery and more products in waves
options.feedback: Fixed date, cut scope, small steps. You catch the spring rush and learn what online customers actually buy before adding the rest.

options.text: Hire extra help and push to get all 2,000 products and delivery live by spring
options.feedback: Spending more to keep full scope and the date is possible, but a big-bang launch at peak season means any failure hits your busiest weeks.

options.text: Skip this spring and launch the complete shop next year
options.feedback: Lower risk and a polished result, but you give up a full season of sales and learning to get it.

cards.title: Fix the date, cut the scope, launch in small steps.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Scope, time and cost:** when the date and budget are fixed, shrink what you deliver. **Small steps vs big bang:** release in pieces so each problem is small and easy to find.
**Try it today:** take one project you're running. Write which of scope, time and cost is truly fixed. Then list what could ship first and what could wait.
